meta.blurb: Leila's money disappears every month and she cannot say why. Over tea, a retired shopkeeper gives her one simple question that sorts everything she owns or owes into assets and liabilities, and then shows her what to do next.
meta.bible: Leila: a young woman of about twenty-two with her first full-time job at a garden centre; curious, honest and a little embarrassed about money. Mr Okafor: her neighbour, about seventy, a retired shopkeeper who ran a small hardware shop for forty years; patient, dry-humoured and kind; he drinks ginger tea and keeps a thick notebook. Money is counted in dollars. Leila's pay is two thousand dollars a month after tax. About four hundred dollars a month went on small things she hardly noticed. Her starting net worth is about minus two thousand dollars: a little over one thousand dollars of savings, laptop and bicycle, against a student loan and phone payments of more than three thousand. A year later her net worth has risen by almost four thousand dollars. Key terms: Asset, Liability, Income, Expenses, Inflation, Interest, Compound, Mortgage, Debt, Diversification, Bond, Bonds, Fund, Share, Shares, Net worth, Emergency fund, Insurance, Tax, Bookkeeping, Carpentry, Programming, Landlady, Tenant, Garden centre. Mr Okafor's shop story: a bright new sign did little, a second fridge for cold drinks paid for itself within a season. The one question: does this put money in my pocket, or take it out? The book teaches general principles only, does not name any real brand or person, and is not personal financial advice; tax rules differ by country. Voice: warm, plain, practical and never preachy; every fact is true and hedged where it depends on the country or the market.

B1B2: Leila has just received her first full pay from the garden centre, and she feels rich for about a day. By the end of the month, however, the money has almost vanished, and she cannot say where it went.
Her neighbour Mr Okafor is seventy and ran a small hardware shop for forty years. One Sunday he sees her frowning at her phone and invites her in for tea.
Mr Okafor takes a clean sheet of paper and writes a single question across the top. He says that if she remembers only one thing, it should be this question.
The question reads, “Does this put money into my pocket, or does it take money out?” It is short enough to ask in a shop, and short enough to remember on the bus.
Something that puts money into your pocket, or grows in value over time, is called an asset. A tree that gives fruit to sell is a simple way to remember one.
Something that takes money out of your pocket is called a liability. A bucket with a small hole in it, dripping coins onto the floor, is a good way to remember one.
Before they go any further, Mr Okafor explains two simple words. Income is the money that comes in each month, and expenses are the money that goes out.
That evening Leila writes down every payment from her bank account for the past month. To her surprise, about four hundred dollars went on small things she hardly noticed.
Mr Okafor tells her that cash in the bank is an asset, because it is safe and she can use it at any time. However, prices usually rise over the years, so the same cash slowly buys less.
Mr Okafor says there is nothing wrong with owning a good phone, because she needs it for work and for friends. The point is not to feel guilty, but to know exactly what it is.
Next Mr Okafor talks about cars, which many young people want very badly. A car needs fuel, repairs and insurance every month, and a car usually loses value as it gets older.
But the same car can be different for a taxi driver, who earns money every day by driving people around town. For her, the car helps to put money into her pocket.
Mr Okafor taps the table and says this is the most important lesson so far. A thing is not an asset or a liability by its name, but by what it does for you.

Leila asks about a home, because her parents say that their house is their greatest asset. Mr Okafor explains that a home costs money every month through repairs, taxes and loan payments, but its price can also rise.
A home rented to someone else can put money into your pocket each month. However, the owner must still pay for repairs, taxes and the time when no one lives there.
Next they talk about debt, a word that worries many young people. Debt is money that you borrow and must pay back later, and in most cases you pay extra for the loan.
Some debts can help a person earn more later, such as a loan for a course that leads to a better job. Many debts, however, only pay for things that lose value, and they still must be repaid.
Credit cards are the example Mr Okafor likes least, because they often charge a very high rate of interest. A small balance can grow quickly if it is not paid back each month.
Mr Okafor explains compound interest by drawing a snowball rolling down a hill. When you owe money, interest is added to the debt, and then more interest is charged on the larger amount.
Then he turns the paper around and shows that the same snowball can work for you. When you save or invest, your earnings can earn more earnings, and the pile grows faster over the years.
A savings account is the simplest asset most people have. It is usually safe, and it pays a small amount of interest, although the rate may be lower than the rise in prices.
Another kind of asset is a share, which is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, the share may become more valuable, but if it does badly, the share can lose value.
A fund puts the shares of many companies together in one basket, so that a person does not need to choose them one by one. If one company fails, the others can still help to hold up the value.
A bond is a loan that you make to a company or a government. In return, you are paid interest for a set time, and you should receive your original money back at the end.
Mr Okafor tells her about his own hardware shop, which was an asset because it earned more than it cost. Then he warns that it was also a lot of hard work, especially in the first few years.
Not every asset is something that you can touch or hold in your hand. A useful skill is an asset, because it can raise the money you earn, and nobody can take it away from you.
Mr Okafor says that good health is another asset that is easy to forget. A person who is well can work, learn and enjoy life, and a person who is not well often spends more money on care.
Mr Okafor says that money comes into a life in three main ways. It can come from work, from a business, or from assets such as savings and shares that earn on their own.
Mr Okafor asks her to take her income and subtract her expenses. The number that remains is the amount she can save or invest, and he calls it the gap.
Mr Okafor says that when people earn more, they often spend more, so the gap stays small. Better flats, bigger cars and nicer meals slowly become normal, and the extra money disappears.
His answer is a simple habit, and he calls it paying yourself first. On the day your pay arrives, move a fixed amount into savings before you spend anything, and live on the rest.

Before she buys any other asset, Mr Okafor says that Leila needs an emergency fund. Many experts suggest three to six months of expenses, so that a lost job or a broken boiler does not become a disaster.
Mr Okafor then introduces net worth, which is the total value of your assets minus the total of your debts. It is a snapshot of where you stand today, not a judgement of who you are.
Leila adds up her savings, laptop and bicycle, and then adds her student loan and phone payments. She owns about one thousand dollars, but she owes more than three thousand.
Mr Okafor tells her not to be afraid of the negative number. Many young people begin adult life owing more than they own, and what matters is the direction the number moves.
Mr Okafor explains that she should look at her debts and find the one with the highest interest. Paying that one off first saves her the most money.

Some people prefer to repay their smallest debt first, because a quick win can keep them going. Mr Okafor says that this costs a little more in interest, but the best plan is the one you will really follow.
Before she buys anything big, Mr Okafor says, Leila should ask whether she needs it or only wants it. Then she should ask what it will cost her over a whole year, not just today.
Mr Okafor gives her three questions for any purchase. Will it earn money, will it keep its value, or is it simply a cost that she is happy to accept?
Years ago, Mr Okafor spent his savings on a bright new sign for his shop, and almost nothing changed. A year later he bought a second fridge for cold drinks, and it paid for itself within a season.
Mr Okafor warns Leila that looking rich is different from being rich. A person with an expensive car, an expensive coat and a big loan may own very little.
Insurance is a cost that protects your assets from large and sudden losses. Mr Okafor says that it is dull to pay for, but it is cheaper than facing a disaster alone.

Mr Okafor says that tax rules differ from one country to another, and they also change over time. He asks Leila to check the rules where she lives, because the same asset can be taxed in very different ways.
Mr Okafor reminds Leila that no asset is completely certain. Prices go up and down, and so the wise way to protect yourself is to spread your money across different kinds of assets.
Mr Okafor says that time is the quiet helper of anyone who owns assets. A tree does not grow in a week, and neither does a pile of savings.
Before she leaves, Leila writes her plan in her notebook. She will track her spending, save a fixed amount on payday, and pay off her costliest debt first.
A year later, Leila opens her notebook and turns through the pages. She did not follow her plan perfectly, but she followed it most months.
Leila adds up what she owns and what she owes, just as before. Her net worth is still small, but it has gone up by almost four thousand dollars.
When her younger brother gets his first job, Leila draws the same question on a clean sheet of paper. She explains it in her own words, and he starts to ask it about everything.

The lesson is simple, and Leila can remember it easily. Ask what each thing does for your money, build assets slowly, and remember that this book is general information and not personal financial advice.
C1C2: When Leila received her first full pay from the garden centre, two thousand dollars after tax, she felt wealthier than she had ever been. Within a few weeks the money had slipped away through a hundred small doors, and she could not have named a single one of them. It puzzled her deeply, because she had worked hard for every dollar and had expected it to stay.

Her neighbour Mr Okafor, who had run a small hardware shop for forty years, noticed her frowning at her phone one Sunday afternoon and invited her in for tea. His kitchen smelled of ginger and old wood, and a thick notebook lay open beside the teapot. “Money is not complicated,” he said, “but nobody ever teaches it to us in plain words.”

Mr Okafor took a clean sheet of paper and wrote a single question across the top in large, careful letters. He told her that most of what people call financial wisdom is simply this one question, asked again and again about everything they own and everything they owe. Leila leaned forward, half expecting something clever, and was surprised by how short it was.

The question read, “Does this put money into my pocket, or does it take money out?” It sounded almost too simple to matter, yet Mr Okafor said that he had spent his whole working life returning to it. Short enough to ask inside a shop and plain enough to remember on a crowded bus, it was meant to be used rather than admired.

Anything that puts money into your pocket, or that can reasonably be expected to grow in value over the years, is called an asset. Mr Okafor drew a small tree on the page and explained that a fruit tree was a perfect example of the idea, since it gives you something to sell each season. Leila noticed that the tree did not need to be sold in order to be useful, and she wrote that down.

A liability, Mr Okafor said, is the opposite: something that takes money out of your pocket, whether once or month after month. He drew a bucket with a small hole in its side and a trail of coins dripping to the floor, and Leila laughed because she suddenly recognised several things in her own life. The drawing was funny, but the idea behind it was serious enough to change how she looked at her wages.

Before going any further, Mr Okafor made sure that two ordinary words were completely clear. Income is the money that arrives each month, whether from a job, a business or a gift, and expenses are everything that leaves again for rent, food, transport and entertainment. The difference between the two, he added, is the quiet number on which the rest of a person's life depends.

That evening Leila sat at her table and copied every payment from her bank account for the past month, line by line, without leaving anything out. To her astonishment, nearly four hundred dollars had gone on small things she barely remembered, such as coffee, deliveries and apps she no longer used. She felt less guilty than curious, as if she had finally switched on a light in a room she had been walking through in the dark.

Cash in a bank account is an asset, Mr Okafor said, because it is safe, it is instantly available, and it often earns a little interest as well. Nevertheless, prices tend to creep upward year after year, a slow change called inflation, and so a pile of cash that never grows will quietly buy less and less. He did not want her to fear cash; he only wanted her to understand what it can and cannot do.

There is nothing shameful about owning a good phone, Mr Okafor reassured her, since she needed one for work, for friends and for daily life. The purpose of his question was never to make her feel guilty but to help her see each thing for what it truly is, so that she could choose with open eyes. A person who knows a cost is a cost, he said, makes better decisions than one who pretends it is an investment.

Next Mr Okafor turned to the example that fascinated every young person he had ever known, which was the car. A car swallows money in fuel, repairs, parking and insurance every single month, and in most cases it is worth a little less each year than it was the year before. For many people it is still a perfectly sensible purchase, he said, as long as they do not mistake it for a way of getting richer.

On the other hand, the very same model of car can behave quite differently in the hands of a taxi driver, who earns her living by carrying passengers across the city. If the money she collects each month is greater than what the car costs her in fuel, repairs and insurance, then it is working for her rather than against her. The object itself had not changed at all, and only the job that it was doing for its owner had changed.

Mr Okafor tapped the table twice, which Leila would learn was his way of marking the most important point of the afternoon. Nothing is an asset or a liability because of what it is called, he said, but because of what it does in your life, month after month, to the money in your pocket. This single idea, she realised, made the whole question more useful than any list could ever be.

Leila asked about homes, because her parents always described their house as the best thing they owned. Mr Okafor chose his words carefully, explaining that a home you live in takes money from you every month through repairs, taxes and mortgage payments, while its price may or may not rise over the years. It can be a store of value and a liability at the same time, he said, and honest people disagree about which side matters more.

A home that is rented to someone else can behave very differently, because the rent arrives in the owner's pocket month after month. Even so, the owner still pays for repairs, for taxes and for those anxious weeks when the flat stands empty, so the rent must be compared with the true costs before anyone can call it profit. Mr Okafor added that rules about renting and taxes differ greatly between countries, and that Leila should always check hers.

Next they talked about debt, a word that had always made Leila's stomach tighten a little whenever she heard it. Mr Okafor said it was nothing more mysterious than money borrowed from someone else, to be paid back at a later date, almost always with an extra charge called interest. Used carefully, debt can open doors, but it is also the quickest way for a liability to grow without anyone noticing.

Some borrowing, Mr Okafor said, is a bet that the loan will lead to something worth more than it costs, such as a course that opens the way to a better job. Other borrowing pays for things that are used up or that lose their value quickly, and yet the payments continue for months or years after the pleasure has faded. Even the sensible kind carries risk, since nobody can promise that the better job will arrive.

Credit cards were the example Mr Okafor liked least, because in many countries they charge interest at a rate far higher than any savings account will ever pay. A small balance left unpaid can therefore swell month after month, until the original purchase is a distant memory and the interest is the main thing being paid. He advised Leila to check the exact rate on any card she was offered, and to read the small print twice.

To explain compound interest, Mr Okafor drew a snowball at the top of a hill and then a much larger one at the bottom. When you owe money, each round of interest is added to the debt, and the next round is calculated on the bigger total, so the amount grows faster as time goes by. This, he said, is why a small debt ignored for a long time can become a heavy one.

Then he turned the paper around and pointed out that the very same snowball could roll in the saver's favour. When money is saved or invested, the earnings are added to the pile and begin to earn earnings of their own, so that growth gathers speed with the years. It was the very same force, Leila realised with a small shock of delight, only now pointing in the opposite direction.

A savings account, Mr Okafor said, is the plainest and most comfortable asset that most people ever own. It is usually safe, it can be reached quickly in an emergency, and it pays a modest amount of interest, although that rate may sometimes fall behind the rising cost of living. For that reason it is wonderful for short-term safety and rather weak as a way to grow wealth over decades.

Another kind of asset is a share, which is simply a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company earns good profits, the share may rise in value and may also pay the owner a regular amount, but if the company struggles, the price can fall sharply. Mr Okafor stressed that a share is an asset only in the sense that it has the chance to reward you, and that no one can promise it will.

Choosing individual companies is difficult, so many people buy a fund, which gathers the shares of a great number of firms in one large basket. Because the money is spread so widely, the failure of a single company hurts far less than it would if everything had been placed in that one business. Mr Okafor explained that this spreading, called diversification, is one of the few free gifts in the world of money.

A bond, Mr Okafor said, turns the idea of debt upside down, because here it is you who lends the money to a company or a government. In return you are promised regular interest for a fixed period and the return of your original sum at the end, although the promise is only as good as the borrower who makes it. Bonds are usually calmer than shares in their ups and downs, but calmer does not mean that they are free of risk.

Mr Okafor spoke fondly of his own hardware shop, which had been an asset for decades because it earned more each month than it cost to keep open. He was honest, however, that in the early years it had demanded every hour of his day, and that a business that depends on one tired owner is only partly the kind of asset that works while you sleep. Many small shops, he added, do not survive their first few years, so nobody should enter that world carelessly.

Not every asset can be held in the hand or placed in a drawer, Mr Okafor reminded her. A useful skill, whether it is bookkeeping, carpentry, programming or simply the ability to explain a hard idea, can raise the money you earn for the rest of your working life, and no thief can ever steal it. Leila thought of the evening class she had been considering and felt a small, pleasant shock of recognition.

Good health, Mr Okafor added, is the asset that people forget until they lose it. A person who is well can work, learn and enjoy the days, whereas illness often reduces income at exactly the moment when costs are rising, so looking after your body is a quiet kind of financial planning. He was careful to say that this is not a promise, since even careful people fall ill, but it is a reasonable habit.

Money comes into a life, Mr Okafor explained, in three main ways, and the differences between them matter a great deal. It may arrive as wages in exchange for your time, as profit from a business you run, or as returns from assets that earn while you are doing something else entirely. Leila's pay slip fell into the first group, and she began to see that most people's financial journeys involve slowly adding the other two.

Mr Okafor asked her to take what she earned each month and subtract everything she spent. The number that was left, he said, is the gap, and it is the raw material of every future asset she will ever own, since only money that is not spent can be turned into something else. If the gap is small, there are only two ways to widen it: earn more or spend less.

There is a trap, Mr Okafor warned, that catches almost everyone who receives a pay rise. Spending quietly climbs to meet the new income, with a nicer flat, a faster phone and dinners out, until the gap is as thin as before and the extra money seems never to have arrived. Because it happens so gradually, it is rarely noticed until several years have already passed.

His answer was a habit with an almost embarrassingly simple name: pay yourself first. On the very day your wages arrive, move a fixed amount into savings before you buy a single thing, and then arrange the rest of the month around what remains. Because the money is out of sight before the temptation begins, you rely on routine instead of willpower, which is a far more dependable resource.

Before buying any other kind of asset, Mr Okafor said, Leila should build an emergency fund, a stock of cash for the day when something unexpected goes wrong. Many financial educators suggest the equivalent of three to six months of basic expenses, although the right figure depends on how secure her job is and who depends on her. Without such a cushion, a lost job or a broken boiler can force a person into expensive debt in a single week.

Mr Okafor then introduced a term that sounded rather grand for such a modest idea: net worth. It is the total value of everything you own, minus the total of everything you owe, and it gives you a single honest snapshot of where you stand on one particular day. He stressed that it describes a position and not a person, and that anyone can change it.

At the kitchen table Leila added up her small savings, her laptop and her bicycle, a little over one thousand dollars, and then her student loan and the remaining phone payments, which came to more than three thousand. When she subtracted the second total from the first, the answer was a negative number of roughly two thousand dollars. Seeing it written in black ink was uncomfortable, but it was also strangely like relief, because at last the problem had a size.

Mr Okafor assured her that she should not be afraid of the negative number, because it was where nearly everyone begins. Students, apprentices and young workers very often owe more than they own, he said, and the only thing that truly matters is the direction in which the figure is moving from one year to the next. A low number that is climbing, he added with a smile, is far better than a high number that is sinking.

To begin climbing, Mr Okafor advised, she should list all of her debts together with the interest rate on each, and then direct any spare money to the one with the highest rate while paying the minimum on the others. This approach usually saves the most money in the end, because the costliest debt is the one that grows fastest. Leila copied the list carefully and felt, for the first time, that she had a plan.

Mr Okafor admitted that some people prefer a different method, which is to repay the smallest debt first so that each early success encourages them to continue. It may cost somewhat more in interest than the first approach, he said, but a plan that a person abandons halfway is worth less than a slightly slower plan that she completes. The best method, in the end, is the one that you will actually follow.

Before buying anything large, Mr Okafor suggested, Leila should ask herself whether it is a need or a want, and then calculate what it will cost over an entire year rather than on the day she pays. Many items look cheap on the price tag but turn out to be expensive once the repairs, the subscriptions and the replacement are counted. This habit takes only a minute, yet it prevents a surprising number of regrets.

Mr Okafor offered her three questions to carry with her into any shop, showroom or website where she was tempted to spend. Will this earn me money, will it keep its value for a long time, or is it a pure cost that I am entirely happy to accept? Any of the three answers can be perfectly fine, he said, provided that she gives the answer honestly and before the payment is made rather than afterwards.

Years ago, Mr Okafor recalled, he had spent a large part of his savings on a magnificent new sign for the front of his shop, and he had been certain that customers would stream through the door. Hardly anything changed, whereas a second fridge for cold drinks, bought the following spring, repaid its cost before the summer was over. He had learned, he said, to ask what a purchase would do rather than how it would look.

Mr Okafor cautioned Leila that appearances can be deeply misleading, since someone who looks rich may merely be someone who spends a great deal. A gleaming car, a fine coat and a large house, all bought on borrowed money, can hide a net worth that is smaller than that of a quiet neighbour who saves a little each month. True wealth, he said, is very often exactly what you cannot see from the street, because it sits quietly in a bank account.

Insurance, Mr Okafor explained, is a peculiar kind of cost, because you pay a regular amount in the hope that you will never need it. Yet it protects your home, your income or your health from a loss so large that it could wipe out years of careful saving, and in that sense it is part of guarding your assets. He told Leila to read the details of any policy and to compare several offers.

Mr Okafor paused to say that everything he described is shaped, in practice, by the tax rules of the country where a person lives, and that those rules differ widely and change from time to time. The same asset can be taxed lightly in one place and heavily in another, so Leila should consult official sources or a qualified adviser before making important decisions. He was only teaching principles, he said, and not giving advice about her own situation.

Not even the best asset is completely certain, Mr Okafor reminded her, for prices fall as well as rise and businesses sometimes fail without warning. The sensible response is not to give up but to spread your money across several kinds of assets, keeping part of it safe and part of it growing, so that no single mistake can undo everything. A person who has all her eggs in one basket, he said, must pray that nobody trips.

Time, Mr Okafor said, is the quiet partner of anyone who owns assets, and it works hardest for those who start early and stay calm. A tree does not grow in a week, and a pile of savings does not turn into security in a month, but a small amount added regularly for many years can become something remarkable. The people who struggle most, he had noticed, are often the ones who expect results too soon.

Before she left, Leila wrote out her plan in her notebook in her neatest handwriting. She would track every payment, move a fixed amount into savings on payday, build a small emergency fund, and send any extra money to the debt that charged her the most interest. It was not a dramatic plan, but she could see exactly how each step would make the next one possible.

A year later, Leila opened her notebook at the kitchen table and turned slowly through twelve months of neat handwriting. There were a few pages where she had overspent and a few where she had not written anything at all, but most of the months showed a small, steady line of progress. She was surprised by how little drama there had been, and how much had changed.

Leila added up everything she owned and everything she owed, exactly as she had done on that first Sunday. The new total was still modest, but it had climbed by almost four thousand dollars, thanks to regular saving, a small pay rise after her evening class, and a smaller student loan. She noticed that the number itself mattered less than the fact that she understood every part of it.

When her younger brother received his first pay slip, Leila took a clean sheet of paper and wrote the same question across the top, in the same careful letters. She explained assets and liabilities in her own words, using the garden centre as her example, and within an hour he was asking of every object on the table whether it put money in or took it out. Passing the idea on, she discovered, was the best way of making it her own.

The lesson, as Mr Okafor had promised on the first day, fits on a single sheet of paper: ask what each thing does for the money in your pocket, and then let the answer guide your choices. Build assets slowly, protect yourself with savings, keep costly debt under control, and be patient with the years. This book offers general information and not personal financial advice, so for important decisions, speak to a qualified adviser in your own country.
